The pre-1900 Thomaston housing inventory is more intact than many comparable west-central Georgia communities. Multi-entry profiles are the rule, not the exception.

bat-removal.extendedBody:
Bat Removal Across Thomaston & Upson County

Bat problems in Thomaston tend to follow the local housing. The older homes near the courthouse square and the former Thomaston Mills mill-village neighborhoods have the masonry chimneys, wood soffits, and louvered gable vents that bats slip behind, while newer builds and rural Upson County properties usually let them in through gaps at the roofline, fascia, and vent screens. Whatever the home, the bats most often roosting in Georgia attics and chimneys are big brown bats, which favor warm, undisturbed spaces and will return to the same roost year after year if the openings are left unsealed.

How Bats Get Into Local Homes

A bat needs only about a half-inch gap to get inside, so the entry points are easy to miss from the ground. The ones our local inspectors find most often in and around Thomaston are:

  • Open or uncapped chimney flues, and gaps where old mortar or the chimney crown has cracked.
  • Soffit and fascia gaps, especially where wood has aged or pulled away at the corners.
  • Louvered gable vents with torn or missing screening behind them.
  • Roofline and ridge gaps, and the seams where a porch, dormer, or addition meets the main roof.

A proper inspection checks all of these before any sealing begins, because closing the wrong gap first can trap the colony inside.

Bat Protection & Removal Rules in Georgia

Bats are protected under Georgia Department of Natural Resources rules, so they cannot be poisoned or trapped — the only legal and effective method is exclusion, which lets the colony leave on its own and then seals them out. Exclusion is not allowed during the maternity season, roughly May through August, when flightless pups would be sealed inside. Some bat species are also under federal review for added protection, so timing and requirements can change; a licensed Georgia operator confirms the current rules before scheduling. You can verify the latest guidance directly with the Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division and the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service. Any bat work in Upson County should be handled by a contractor licensed under Georgia DNR — not a general handyman.

Guano Cleanup in Older Thomaston Homes

When a colony has used an attic or chimney for a long time, the droppings (guano) build up — and dried guano can carry the spores that cause histoplasmosis, a lung infection. That is why cleanup matters as much as the removal itself, and why droppings should never be swept or vacuumed by a homeowner. A licensed crew contains the area, removes the contaminated material and any soiled insulation using proper protective equipment, sanitizes the space, and seals the entry points so a new colony can't move back in. Older homes with long-used chimneys generally need more cleanup than a recent build, which is the main reason a full job costs more than the exclusion alone.

faqs.q: How much does bat removal cost in Thomaston?
faqs.a: Bat exclusion in Thomaston typically runs $400–$1,500+ for the exclusion work itself. If a colony has left guano that needs cleanup and attic decontamination, expect an additional $1,500–$8,000+ depending on the colony's size and how long it has been roosting. Older homes with long-used chimneys tend to fall at the higher end. Call for a free on-site estimate.

faqs.q: When can bats be legally excluded in Thomaston?
faqs.a: Bat exclusion in Georgia is paused during the maternity season — roughly May through August — when flightless pups would be trapped inside. Outside that window is the time to do the work. Because some species are also under federal review, a licensed operator confirms the current timing first. We can inspect and prepare your Thomaston home any time so work starts the moment the window opens.

faqs.q: Are the bats in my Thomaston attic protected?
faqs.a: Yes. Bats are protected under Georgia DNR rules, so they can't legally be killed, poisoned, or trapped. The approved method is exclusion: one-way devices let the colony fly out and prevent it from returning, after which the entry points are sealed. You can confirm current protections with the Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division or the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service.

faqs.q: Is bat guano in my Thomaston home dangerous?
faqs.a: It can be. Dried bat guano can carry spores of the fungus that causes histoplasmosis, a respiratory illness. Don't sweep, vacuum, or disturb droppings in your attic or chimney — that sends spores into the air. A licensed crew cleans the contaminated material under containment with respiratory protection, then sanitizes and seals the space so the problem doesn't return.

faqs.q: I found a bat inside my Thomaston house — does that mean there's a colony?
faqs.a: Often, yes. A single bat in living space usually slipped in from a colony roosting in the attic, a wall void, or a chimney. An inspection can tell you whether there's a larger group above the ceiling. If the bat may have had contact with a sleeping person, child, or pet, call Georgia DNR or your county health department about rabies testing.

faqs.q: Can I seal the entry points myself?
faqs.a: It's risky and often illegal. Sealing gaps without timed one-way exclusion traps bats — and during the May–August maternity season, their pups — inside the walls, where they die and cause odor and contamination. You also risk histoplasmosis exposure from disturbed guano. A licensed Thomaston specialist handles the timing, cleanup, and permanent sealing so it's done once, correctly, and legally.
